prompt: What does setting `requires_grad = False` on a parameter tensor change during training?
hint: Look at the list of tensors that had a gradient after backward.

choices.text: The layer is skipped in the forward pass
choices.why: It still runs; the convolutions computed their outputs and the gradient flowed through them.

choices.text: Backward stores no gradient for it, so the step leaves it alone
choices.why: Right. Backward left `.grad` empty for the four convolution tensors, and the step did not change them.

choices.text: The layer switches to evaluation mode, as `model.eval()` does
choices.why: The two are unrelated: eval mode changes dropout and batch normalisation, and says nothing about gradients.

choices.text: The optimiser deletes it from its parameter groups
choices.why: The optimiser holds whatever list it was given; a tensor with no gradient is simply skipped.

prompt: A colleague calls `model.eval()` on a pretrained body to freeze it, then trains with an optimiser holding every parameter. What happens to the body?
hint: `freeze.py` ran backward in evaluation mode.

choices.text: It stays fixed, because eval mode turns gradients off
choices.why: That is the belief the section tests; the gradients arrived in eval mode regardless.

choices.text: Training stops with an error on the first batch
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; backward and the step run as usual.

choices.text: It keeps learning; its tensors still get gradients
choices.why: Right. Freezing is `requires_grad = False`, or leaving the tensors out of the optimiser.

choices.text: Only its batch normalisation layers keep learning
choices.why: Eval mode stops batch normalisation updating its running statistics; it does not stop any gradient.

prompt: In `freeze.py`, the network has 37,957 parameters and learns 33,157. How many parameters do the two frozen convolutions hold?
hint: Add the four `requires_grad=False` rows, or subtract.

prompt: Why does every pretrained start in `depths.py` get a new head instead of keeping `base.pt`'s?
hint: What does each output of the old head stand for?

choices.text: The old head's weights are not saved in `base.pt`
choices.why: They are, as `8.weight` and `8.bias`; `forget.py` puts them back later.

choices.text: Its five outputs mean 0 to 4, not the new digits
choices.why: Right. A head is tied to the labels of one task, so a new task gets a new one.

choices.text: A new head trains faster than a loaded one
choices.why: It trains the same way, 325 parameters either way; what differs is what its outputs mean.

choices.text: PyTorch refuses to train a layer loaded from a file
choices.why: The last block and everything train loaded layers in the same run.

prompt: With 10 images per class, how did fine-tuning everything compare with training from scratch?
hint: The `scratch` and `everything` rows of the middle block.

choices.text: Clearly ahead, near 0.98 on each seed
choices.why: No run with 10 per class reached that; 0.98 belongs to scratch with 50.

choices.text: Level with the head-alone start
choices.why: The head alone stayed at 0.672 to 0.689, far below.

choices.text: It did not train and stayed near chance
choices.why: Chance among five digits is 0.2, and it scored above 0.9.

choices.text: A little behind: 0.917 to 0.933 against 0.933 to 0.944
choices.why: Right. Close, and still not ahead, because this donor has little to give.

prompt: Put the lesson's recipe for choosing how much of a pretrained network to fine-tune in order.
hint: The cheapest comparison comes first, and the baseline before all of them.
items: Train the same network from scratch as the baseline
Train only a new head on the frozen body
Unfreeze the last block as well
Keep the depth the validation score says earned its parameters

prompt: You have a body pretrained on millions of plant photographs and 30 new photographs of a leaf disease that look much like the donor's. Which start does the lesson suggest trying hardest?
hint: Few images to fit, and features that are probably still general.

choices.text: A frozen depth, starting with the head only
choices.why: Right. Every parameter that learns is fitted to 30 images, and a large, similar donor's features are worth keeping.

choices.text: Everything at a high rate, which did best in `rates.py`
choices.why: It did best there because `base.pt` had little to give; here the donor has a lot.

choices.text: Scratch alone, since scratch won in this lesson
choices.why: It won against a 528-image donor; a network trained from scratch on 30 photographs is poor.

choices.text: Everything with the head left frozen
choices.why: The new head starts random and is the one part that must learn.

prompt: Giving the layers near the input a lower rate than the layers near the head is called ___ fine-tuning.
hint: The word is in the last part of the section.

prompt: In `rates.py`, what did the number in brackets do as the rate went from 1e-4 to 1e-2?
hint: It compares the first layer with `base.pt`.

choices.text: It fell, as the old digits were forgotten
choices.why: The old digits are measured in `forget.py`; this number is a distance between weights.

choices.text: It grew, from about 0.04 to about 0.4 of its size
choices.why: Right. The higher the rate, the further the first layer travelled from what `base.pt` gave it.

choices.text: It stayed at zero, since the first layer was frozen
choices.why: Every layer learnt in `rates.py`; the slowest setup still moved it 0.04.

choices.text: It tracked the final loss
choices.why: The loss is not printed; `moved()` compares two weight tensors.

prompt: With a body pretrained on far more data than you have, why do the layers near the input usually get the smallest rate?
hint: What do those layers hold, and what did it cost to learn?

choices.text: They hold the most parameters, so each step must be smaller
choices.why: Here the two convolutions hold 4,800 of 37,957; the rate follows what a layer knows, not its size.

choices.text: Their gradients are the largest in the network
choices.why: Lesson 3 saw gradients shrink towards the input in a deep sigmoid network, not grow.

choices.text: Their general features took more data than you have
choices.why: Right. Each step away from them throws away something your data could not teach again.

choices.text: A lower rate makes each epoch run faster
choices.why: The rate changes the size of a step, not what a step costs to compute.

prompt: How does `forget.py` measure what the fine-tuned body still knows about the digits 0 to 4?
hint: Look at `old_task`.

choices.text: It trains a fresh head on 0 to 4 after fine-tuning
choices.why: A fresh head could relearn a lot from a changed body and hide the damage; the old one cannot.

choices.text: It measures how far the weights moved from `base.pt`
choices.why: That is `rates.py`'s `moved()`; a distance does not say what still works.

choices.text: It puts `base.pt`'s own head back and scores 0 to 4
choices.why: Right. If the body still computes what that head expects, the old digits are still recognised.

choices.text: It counts the units that stay silent on 0 to 4
choices.why: Counting silent units was lesson 13's check, on the new digits.

prompt: In `forget.py`, which setup scored best on the new digits, and what did that cost?
hint: Compare the last column with the column for epoch 100.

choices.text: Everything at 1e-2, which lost 0 to 4
choices.why: Right: 0.922 on 5 to 9, while 0 to 4 fell to 0.294. The setup that moved the body furthest learnt the new task best and lost the old one.

choices.text: Head alone, which also kept 0 to 4 at 0.989
choices.why: It kept the old task and scored lowest on the new one, 0.667.

choices.text: Body 1e-4, head 1e-3, at no cost to 0 to 4
choices.why: It kept 0 to 4, and paid with 0.822 on the new digits.

choices.text: The last block, with no loss
choices.why: It reached 0.900, and 0 to 4 eroded to 0.944.

prompt: A shop's model recognises 40 products. You fine-tune all its layers at a high rate on photographs of 5 new products only, keeping the old head aside. What does the lesson predict for the 40 old products?
hint: What in the loss asks the body to keep them?

choices.text: They stay as they were, since their head was not trained
choices.why: The head is untouched, but it reads a body that was rewritten; that is what `forget.py` measured.

choices.text: They improve, from seeing more photos
choices.why: The new photographs pull the body towards the new products, not the old.

choices.text: Nothing, until the new products' accuracy is known
choices.why: The old task can be measured on its own, as `forget.py` does every few epochs.

choices.text: Their accuracy falls sharply, as 0 to 4 did at 1e-2
choices.why: Right. Nothing in the training asks the body to keep the old job, so a high rate rewrites it.

prompt: Why does the `LoRA` class start `B` at zero?
hint: What is `B A` when `B` is zero?

choices.text: So the adapter has nothing to train at the start
choices.why: `A` and `B` both train from the first step; zero is only where `B` begins.

choices.text: So it starts as the pretrained network
choices.why: Right. `B A` is zero, so the layer computes what `W` did, with no random jolt.

choices.text: Because a low-rank matrix has to start at zero
choices.why: `A` is low-rank too and starts random.

choices.text: To cancel the frozen weight `W` in the output
choices.why: `W` stays in the output; `base(x)` is added to the adapter's term.

prompt: Match each matrix of the rank-4 adapter on the 512-to-64 layer to its shape and role.
hint: 64 outputs, 512 inputs, rank 4.

prompt: After `adapt.py`, you need the original network back for the digits 0 to 4. What does the run show is enough?
hint: The last two lines of the output.

choices.text: Retraining the old head on 0 to 4 with the adapter on
choices.why: No retraining was needed; with the adapter on the old task scored 0.950 and it was not retrained.

choices.text: Putting the frozen layer back in place of the adapter
choices.why: Right. 0 to 4 scored 0.989 again, because `W` was never overwritten.

choices.text: Merging the adapter, which restores the original weights
choices.why: Merging adds `B A` into `W`; it gives the adapted layer, not the original.

choices.text: It is lost; fine-tuning overwrote the layer
choices.why: That is what full fine-tuning does; LoRA left the layer frozen underneath.

prompt: What does QLoRA change compared with plain LoRA?
hint: Which of the two parts is stored in 4 bits?

choices.text: The adapter is in 4 bits
choices.why: The other way round: the adapter stays in 16 bits so it can learn finely.

choices.text: The frozen base is kept in 4 bits
choices.why: Right: 3.1 GiB instead of 12.6 in `sizes.py`, and the adapter still trains in 16 bits.

choices.text: Every weight is trained, but each is kept in 4 bits
choices.why: The base stays frozen in QLoRA, as in LoRA; only the adapter learns.

choices.text: The base model is deleted and only the adapter is kept
choices.why: The adapter only works beside the base it was trained on.

prompt: You fine-tune a chat model on your company's support tickets, and afterwards it answers general questions worse. Which change addresses that most directly?
hint: The same defences as `forget.py`'s digits.

choices.text: Raise the learning rate so training finishes sooner
choices.why: A higher rate moved `base.pt` furthest and forgot the most.

choices.text: Train more epochs on the tickets alone
choices.why: More steps aimed only at the tickets pull further from the general task.

choices.text: Unfreeze every layer so it can relearn the general answers
choices.why: Nothing in the ticket data teaches general answers; unfreezing more only moves more.

choices.text: A lower rate on a LoRA adapter, with some general text mixed in
choices.why: Right. Each part limits how far the base moves or asks the loss to keep the old task.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson's runs show? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each against a transcript.

choices.text: Fine-tuning everything at 1e-2 left 0 to 4 at 0.294
choices.why: Yes, from 0.989 before the first epoch.

choices.text: Fine-tuning everything beat scratch with 50 images per class
A rank-4 adapter matched the last block, training 2,629 parameters
choices.why: Yes, against 33,157 for the last block.

choices.text: `model.eval()` stopped the body receiving gradients
choices.why: No: four tensors got gradients in evaluation mode.

choices.text: The rows repeated from lesson 13 gave lesson 13's numbers
choices.why: Yes, to the last digit, with the same images and seeds.

prompt: In `adapt.py` at rank 4, which parameters does the optimiser receive?
hint: Everything in `base.pt` was frozen before the adapter and the head were added.

choices.text: All 37,957 of `base.pt`, plus the adapter
choices.why: The loop over `model.parameters()` froze every one of those first.

choices.text: Only `A` and `B`; the new head stays frozen
choices.why: A new `nn.Linear` starts with `requires_grad=True`, so the head learns.

choices.text: `A`, `B` and the new head: 2,629 in all
choices.why: Right: 2,048 plus 256 plus 325.

choices.text: The 512-to-64 weight and the new head
choices.why: That is the last block of `depths.py`; here the weight stays frozen inside the adapter.
